back_translation: The words of the Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem
“Utterly without substance,” says the Teacher, “utterly without substance — everything is without substance.”
What gain does man get from all his toil, at which he toils under the sun?
One generation passes away and another generation comes in, but the earth remains forever.
The sun rises and the sun sets, and hurries to the place from which it rose.
The wind blows to the south and circles to the north; it circles round and round, and the wind returns to its former course.
All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full; to the place from which the rivers flow, there they flow back again.
All things are wearisome, more than anyone can describe; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun.
Is there anything of which it can be said, “Behold, this is new”? It has existed long ago, in the ages before us.
There is no remembrance of the former generations, and the later generations to come will likewise not be remembered by those who come after.
I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I set my heart to seek and explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven. This is a burdensome task that God has given to the sons of men to be occupied with.
I have seen all the works that are done under the sun, and behold, everything is without substance — a chasing after the wind.
What is crooked cannot be stretched straight, and what is lacking cannot be fully counted.
I said within my heart, “Behold, I have become great and increased in wisdom more than all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge.”
So I set my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly; I learned that this too is a chasing after the wind.
For where there is much wisdom there is much sorrow, and he who increases knowledge increases pain.
